chapter: Chemical Reactions and Equations (Class 10 Science, CBSE)
note: Authored MCQs, 40 per concept, 14 Easy / 13 Medium / 13 Hard.

2724.stem: In a word equation, the substances written on the left of the arrow are the
2724.explanation: The left-hand side of a word equation always lists the reactants, the substances present before the reaction.

options.why: Products are written on the right, after the arrow.
A catalyst is written above the arrow, not on either side.
A solvent is a medium, and is usually not shown in a word equation at all.

2724.stem: The arrow in a word equation is read as
2724.explanation: The arrow means 'gives' or 'yields' and always points from reactants towards products.

options.why: An equals sign implies no direction, but a reaction proceeds one way.
Confuses a chemical arrow with a mathematical inequality.
Addition between substances is shown by the plus sign, not the arrow.

2724.stem: Magnesium reacts with oxygen to give magnesium oxide. The correct word equation is
2724.explanation: Reactants go on the left joined by a plus sign, and the single product goes on the right of the arrow.

options.why: Reverses the reaction, describing decomposition instead of combination.
Places a reactant on the product side, so oxygen appears to be made.
Treats the product as a reactant, which the description does not say.

2724.stem: Two reactants in a word equation are separated by
2724.explanation: A plus sign separates substances on the same side of a word equation.

options.why: The arrow separates the two sides, not substances within a side.
Commas are not used in the standard form of a word equation.
A full stop would end the equation rather than join substances.

2724.stem: A word equation shows the names of substances but does NOT show their
2724.explanation: Word equations give no formulae and therefore no information about the relative amounts or masses involved.

options.why: The names of the substances are exactly what a word equation does give.
Reactants on the left and products on the right are clearly shown.
The arrow shows the direction plainly.

2724.stem: Zinc + Sulphuric acid -> Zinc sulphate + Hydrogen. The products in this word equation are
2724.explanation: Everything written after the arrow is a product, so zinc sulphate and hydrogen are the products.

options.why: These are on the left of the arrow and so are the reactants.
Mixes one reactant with one product.
Mixes one reactant with one product.

2724.stem: Which of the following is written correctly as a word equation?
2724.explanation: Reactants joined by a plus sign on the left, an arrow, then products on the right is the standard form.

options.why: Uses an equals sign, which does not show the direction of the change.
Uses two arrows, implying two separate steps that are not described.
Uses a comma where a plus sign is required.

2724.stem: The word equation for the rusting of iron in moist air begins with the reactants
2724.explanation: Rusting requires both oxygen from the air and water, so iron, oxygen and water are the reactants.

options.why: Iron does not rust in dry air; water is essential.
Iron does not rust in boiled, air-free water; oxygen is essential.
Carbon dioxide plays no part in ordinary rusting.

2724.stem: What is the chief advantage of a word equation over a sentence?
2724.explanation: A word equation states the same information far more briefly and shows at a glance what changes into what.

options.why: Masses require formulae and balancing, which word equations do not provide.

options.text: It shows the speed of reaction
options.why: Rate is not shown in any kind of equation.
An equation records a reaction; only experiment can prove it occurs.

2724.stem: In the word equation Calcium oxide + Water -> Calcium hydroxide, the number of reactants is
2724.explanation: Two substances appear before the arrow, so there are two reactants and one product.

options.why: Counts only the first substance and misses the second.
Counts the product as a reactant as well.
Counts every name in the equation rather than only those on the left.

2724.stem: Which statement about a word equation is true?
2724.explanation: A word equation never needs balancing, because it contains no symbols or numbers of atoms.

options.text: It does not need to be balanced

options.why: Balancing applies only to equations written with formulae.
States are shown by symbols such as (s) and (aq), which word equations omit.
A catalyst is included only when it is worth noting, and often is not.

2724.stem: Lead nitrate solution reacts with potassium iodide solution. The word equation product that is a solid is
2724.explanation: Lead iodide is insoluble and separates out as a bright yellow precipitate.

options.why: Potassium nitrate is soluble and stays in solution.
This is a reactant, not a product.
This is a reactant, not a product.

2724.stem: A word equation cannot be used to work out
2724.explanation: Because it carries no formulae, a word equation gives no basis for calculating how much of anything reacts.

options.text: how much of each substance reacts

options.why: The names of the reactants are stated explicitly.
The names of the products are stated explicitly.
The arrow gives the direction unambiguously.

2724.stem: The plus sign on the product side of a word equation means the products are
2724.explanation: A plus sign on the right simply means that more than one product is formed together in the reaction.

options.why: Reverses the meaning: the products are results, not things being combined.
Amounts require formulae and balancing to determine.
Products are often in different states, such as a solid and a solution.

2724.stem: Sodium metal dropped into water gives sodium hydroxide and a gas that pops. The correct word equation is
2724.explanation: The gas that burns with a pop is hydrogen, so both products are sodium hydroxide and hydrogen.

options.why: Oxygen rekindles a glowing splint; it does not pop.
Sodium hydroxide forms in water, not the oxide.
Places a product on the reactant side and omits water entirely.

2724.stem: 'Copper oxide reacts with hydrogen to form copper and water.' The reactant that is reduced is
2724.explanation: Copper oxide loses its oxygen to hydrogen, and loss of oxygen is reduction.

options.why: Hydrogen gains oxygen to become water, so it is oxidised, not reduced.
Copper is a product, and a product is not described as reduced.
Water is a product of the change, not a reactant undergoing it.

2724.stem: Which word equation correctly describes the thermal decomposition of limestone?
2724.explanation: Heating calcium carbonate breaks it into calcium oxide and carbon dioxide, so one reactant gives two products.

options.text: Calcium carbonate -> Calcium oxide + Carbon dioxide
Calcium oxide + Carbon dioxide -> Calcium carbonate
options.why: This is the reverse combination reaction, not decomposition.
Calcium hydroxide forms from calcium oxide and water, not from heating alone.
Decomposition here gives simpler compounds, not the free elements.

2724.stem: In which word equation is a metal displacing another metal?
2724.explanation: Iron, being more reactive than copper, takes copper's place in copper sulphate solution.

options.text: Iron + Copper sulphate -> Iron sulphate + Copper

options.why: This is combination with a non-metal, not displacement of a metal.

options.text: Copper carbonate -> Copper oxide + Carbon dioxide
options.why: A single compound splitting up is decomposition.
Two compounds exchanging parts is double displacement, not metal displacement.

2724.stem: A student writes: 'Hydrogen + Chlorine -> Hydrogen chloride + Heat'. The word 'Heat' here
2724.explanation: Heat is energy released by the reaction, not a chemical substance, so writing it as a product is acceptable shorthand for exothermic but it is not a chemical product.

options.text: records energy released, not a substance

options.why: Heat is a form of energy and has no chemical formula.
Heat on the product side indicates release; heat needed would appear on the left.
Reversibility is shown by a double arrow, not by mentioning heat.

2724.stem: Barium chloride solution and sodium sulphate solution give a white precipitate. The word equation product that is white and insoluble is
2724.explanation: The ions exchange partners and barium sulphate, which is insoluble, separates out as a white solid.

options.why: Sodium chloride is soluble and remains dissolved in the mixture.
This is a reactant, and it is soluble.
This is a reactant, and it is soluble.

2724.stem: Which of these sentences would produce a word equation with THREE reactants?
2724.explanation: Rusting needs iron, oxygen and water together, so all three appear on the left of the arrow.

options.text: Iron rusts in the presence of air and moisture
Zinc reacts with dilute hydrochloric acid
options.why: Only two substances are named on the reactant side.
Only one reactant is present; heat is energy, not a substance.
Only one reactant is present; sunlight supplies energy.

2724.stem: Converting the sentence 'quick lime reacts vigorously with water producing slaked lime' into a word equation, the product is
2724.explanation: Slaked lime is the common name for calcium hydroxide, the single product of this combination.

options.why: Calcium oxide is quick lime, which is the reactant here.
Calcium carbonate forms later, when slaked lime meets carbon dioxide from the air.
No chlorine is present anywhere in this reaction.

2724.stem: A word equation is written with the product on the left and the reactants on the right. The equation is
2724.explanation: The convention is fixed: reactants on the left, products on the right, so reversing the sides describes the opposite reaction.

options.why: Direction matters; the two reactions are chemically distinct.
It is meaningful, but it means the opposite of what was intended.

options.text: correct, because sides can be swapped
options.why: The sides of a chemical equation are not interchangeable as they are in algebra.

2724.stem: 'Potassium bromide + Barium iodide -> Potassium iodide + Barium bromide'. This word equation shows
2724.explanation: Each compound has exchanged its partner with the other, which is the defining pattern of a double displacement reaction.

options.text: an exchange of partners between two compounds

options.why: No free element appears anywhere in this equation.
Two compounds go in and two come out, so nothing has split.

options.text: two elements joining into one compound
options.why: There are no free elements among the reactants.

2724.stem: Which sentence would give a word equation with only ONE product?
2724.explanation: Hydrogen and chlorine combine to give hydrogen chloride alone, so the product side has a single substance.

options.text: Hydrogen burns in chlorine to form hydrogen chloride
Zinc reacts with acid giving a salt and a gas
options.why: Two products are named explicitly.

options.text: Lead nitrate is heated giving three substances
options.why: Three products are named explicitly.

options.text: Water is electrolysed to its elements
options.why: Two products, hydrogen and oxygen, are formed.

2724.stem: The main limitation that forces chemists to move from word equations to symbol equations is
2724.explanation: Word equations cannot express how many particles of each substance react, so quantitative work is impossible with them.

options.text: they are difficult to read aloud
options.why: Word equations are actually the easier of the two to read.
Naming the substances is precisely what they do.
Two or more products are shown easily with plus signs.

2724.stem: In 'Lead + Copper chloride -> Lead chloride + Copper', the element displaced is
2724.explanation: Lead takes the place of copper in the chloride, so copper is set free as the displaced element.

options.why: Lead is the displacing metal, since it is the more reactive of the two.
Chlorine stays combined throughout and simply changes partner.
Free copper appears on the product side, which is displacement by definition.

2724.stem: A student writes 'Iron + Copper sulphate -> Copper + Iron sulphate' and also 'Copper + Iron sulphate -> Iron + Copper sulphate', claiming both are valid. The correct assessment is
2724.explanation: Only the first occurs: displacement requires the more reactive metal to displace the less reactive one, and copper cannot displace iron.

options.text: only the first is valid, on reactivity grounds
both are valid, since equations reverse freely
options.why: Chemical equations are not algebraic identities; direction is determined by reactivity.
Inverts the reactivity series, in which iron sits above copper.

options.text: neither is valid, as both are unbalanced
options.why: Balancing is a separate matter and does not decide which direction occurs.

2724.stem: Two word equations are proposed for heating a green copper compound: one gives copper oxide and carbon dioxide, the other gives copper and oxygen. Deciding between them requires knowing
2724.explanation: The identity of the starting compound determines which products are possible: a carbonate can release carbon dioxide, an oxide cannot.

options.text: the identity of the starting compound
the mass of the sample taken
options.why: Mass affects how much product forms, never which products form.

options.text: the colour of the flame used
options.why: The flame supplies heat and does not change the chemistry.
Duration affects completeness, not the identity of the products.

2724.stem: A word equation shows two reactants and two products, with no free element anywhere. This pattern rules out
2724.explanation: A displacement reaction must produce a free element, so the absence of any free element eliminates displacement.

options.why: Double displacement has exactly this pattern of two compounds in and two out.
Precipitation is a double displacement and fits the pattern well.
Acid plus base giving salt plus water fits the pattern exactly.

2724.stem: Why can a word equation be correct as written and still be useless for calculating a yield?
2724.explanation: Correctness of a word equation concerns identity only; yield calculations need formulae and coefficients, which word equations do not carry.

options.text: It states identities but no proportions
It may have the arrow pointing the wrong way
options.why: That would make it incorrect, whereas the question stipulates it is correct.
A catalyst does not appear in yield calculations in any case.

options.text: It uses common names instead of chemical names
options.why: Common names can be translated; the missing proportions cannot.

2724.stem: A student claims a word equation with heat written on the left is always endothermic. The most accurate response is
2724.explanation: Heat on the reactant side means energy must be supplied for the reaction to proceed, which is what endothermic means, so the claim holds for this convention.

options.text: correct, since heat supplied means energy absorbed
wrong, since heat is never written in equations
options.why: Heat is routinely written to show energy supplied or released.

options.text: wrong, since all reactions need some heat to start
options.why: Confuses activation energy with the overall energy change.

options.text: correct, but only for decomposition reactions
options.why: The convention applies to every type of reaction, not just decomposition.

2724.stem: Translating 'silver chloride turns grey in sunlight' into a word equation, the greatest risk of error is
2724.explanation: The grey colour is silver metal, and chlorine is released as a gas; writing 'grey silver chloride' as the product misses that a decomposition occurred.

options.text: treating the grey solid as unchanged silver chloride

options.why: Writing the condition above the arrow is standard and correct practice.

options.text: putting silver chloride on the left
options.why: Silver chloride is the reactant, so the left is exactly where it belongs.

options.text: using an arrow rather than an equals sign
options.why: The arrow is the correct symbol in a chemical equation.

2724.stem: Two students describe the same experiment. One writes three reactants, the other two. The most likely legitimate reason is that
2724.explanation: One student has probably included a substance such as water or air that genuinely takes part, while the other has treated it as merely the surroundings.

options.text: one included a participant the other treated as surroundings

options.why: Possible, but not the most likely legitimate reason when both descriptions can be defensible.

options.text: word equations allow any number of reactants
options.why: They allow any number, but the number should match the chemistry.

options.text: the reaction has no fixed reactants
options.why: A given reaction has definite reactants; only the description varies.

2724.stem: A word equation is written as 'Reactant -> Product A + Product B + Product C'. Which reaction type does this most strongly suggest?
2724.explanation: A single reactant giving several products is the signature of a decomposition reaction.

options.why: Combination goes the other way, with several reactants giving one product.
Displacement needs at least two reactants, one of them a free element.
Double displacement needs two reactants and gives two products.

2724.stem: Which criticism of the word equation 'Acid + Base -> Salt + Water' is the strongest?
2724.explanation: It names classes of substances rather than particular ones, so it describes a pattern rather than any single reaction.

options.text: It names classes, not particular substances
It has the arrow the wrong way round
options.why: Acid and base are the reactants, so the arrow points correctly.
Two products is exactly right for a neutralisation.

options.text: Salt and water cannot form together
options.why: They always form together in a neutralisation.

2724.stem: A student converts 'zinc reacts with sodium hydroxide solution giving hydrogen' into a word equation but cannot name the other product. The best approach is to
2724.explanation: Naming the metal-containing product from the reactants, sodium zincate, completes the equation without guessing at anything not implied.

options.text: deduce the remaining product from the reactants present
leave the product side with hydrogen alone
options.why: The zinc atoms must go somewhere; an incomplete product side is simply wrong.
The product is deducible, so recording ignorance is avoidable.

options.text: write zinc oxide as the product
options.why: Zinc oxide would require oxygen from elsewhere and ignores the sodium.

2724.stem: Why does 'Magnesium + Oxygen -> Magnesium oxide' remain a valid word equation even though it is not balanced?
2724.explanation: Balancing is meaningful only for symbol equations, which count atoms; word equations carry no atom counts at all.

options.text: Word equations carry no atom counts to balance
This reaction happens to be balanced already
options.why: Balance cannot even be assessed without formulae.
Balancing applies to every symbol equation regardless of type.

options.text: Oxygen does not need to be balanced
options.why: In a symbol equation oxygen is balanced like every other element.

2724.stem: A textbook gives 'Photosynthesis: Carbon dioxide + Water -> Glucose + Oxygen'. The most important thing this word equation hides is
2724.explanation: The reaction requires sunlight and chlorophyll, and without these conditions written above the arrow the equation looks like a change that would happen on its own.

options.text: the light and chlorophyll it requires
that carbon dioxide is a gas
options.why: Physical state is minor here and can be added with state symbols.
The chemical class of the product is not essential to the equation.

options.text: that the reaction happens in leaves
options.why: Location is biological context, not chemical information the equation should carry.

2724.stem: Two word equations for the same reaction differ only in that one names a substance by its common name and the other by its chemical name. The correct conclusion is that
2724.explanation: Common and chemical names can refer to the same substance, so both equations describe the same chemistry; only the chemical name is unambiguous.

options.text: both are valid, but the chemical name is unambiguous
only the chemical name version is valid
options.why: Common names such as quick lime are accepted in word equations.
Two names for one substance do not make two reactions.
Common names are familiar but often ambiguous across regions and contexts.

2725.stem: The substances that are used up during a chemical reaction are called
2725.explanation: Reactants are the starting substances that are consumed as the reaction proceeds.

options.why: Products are formed, not used up.
A catalyst is recovered unchanged at the end.
A residue is left behind after a physical separation such as filtering.

2725.stem: In the reaction 2Mg + O2 -> 2MgO, magnesium oxide is
2725.explanation: Magnesium oxide appears after the arrow, so it is the product of the reaction.

options.why: Reactants are magnesium and oxygen, both on the left.
It is formed during the reaction, so it cannot be a catalyst.
No solvent is involved in the burning of magnesium in air.

2725.stem: A catalyst differs from a reactant because a catalyst
2725.explanation: A catalyst speeds a reaction up but is recovered unchanged in mass and composition at the end.

options.text: is recovered unchanged at the end

options.why: Catalysts can be solids, such as iron in the Haber process.
It appears above the arrow, not on either side.
Being used up is the behaviour of a reactant, not a catalyst.

2725.stem: Which of these is a product in the reaction between zinc and dilute sulphuric acid?
2725.explanation: Zinc displaces hydrogen from the acid, so hydrogen gas and zinc sulphate are the products.

options.why: Zinc is the metal that reacts, so it is a reactant.
The acid is consumed, so it is a reactant.
No oxygen gas is produced in this reaction.

2725.stem: During a reaction, the total mass of the reactants compared with the total mass of the products is
2725.explanation: Mass is conserved, so the total mass of the reactants equals the total mass of the products in a closed system.

options.why: Suggests matter is destroyed, which never happens in a chemical reaction.
Suggests matter is created, which never happens in a chemical reaction.
The two are related exactly, by the law of conservation of mass.

2725.stem: In CaCO3 -> CaO + CO2, the number of products is
2725.explanation: Two substances appear on the right of the arrow, so there are two products and one reactant.

options.why: Counts only the first substance on the right.
Counts the reactant along with the products.
Two substances clearly appear after the arrow.

2725.stem: Which statement about reactants and products is correct?
2725.explanation: Products have properties different from the reactants because their atoms are joined in new ways.

options.text: Products have different properties from the reactants
Products always weigh more than the reactants
options.why: Total mass is conserved, so neither side gains overall.
Products may be gases, liquids or solutions.

options.text: Products are always fewer in number
options.why: Decomposition gives more products than reactants.

2725.stem: The substance written above the arrow in an equation is usually
2725.explanation: Conditions such as a catalyst, heat or light are written above the arrow rather than on either side.

options.text: a condition such as a catalyst

options.why: Reactants belong on the left of the arrow.
Products belong on the right of the arrow.
Reaction names are not written into equations.

2725.stem: In the rusting of iron, one of the reactants that is often forgotten is
2725.explanation: Water is essential for rusting, and iron will not rust in perfectly dry air however much oxygen is present.

options.why: Iron is the obvious reactant and is rarely forgotten.
Rust is the product of the reaction.
Nitrogen in the air takes no part in rusting.

2725.stem: A substance present at the start and still present unchanged at the end is
2725.explanation: A catalyst takes part in the mechanism but is regenerated, so it ends the reaction unchanged.

options.why: A reactant is consumed, so it is not present unchanged.
A product was not present at the start.
An impurity is unrelated to the reaction and is not what the term describes.

2725.stem: In a precipitation reaction, the precipitate is always
2725.explanation: The precipitate is the insoluble solid formed during the reaction, so it is one of the products.

options.why: It did not exist before the two solutions were mixed.
It is formed by the reaction and is not recovered unchanged.
The solvent is the liquid, usually water, in which the reaction happens.

2725.stem: Which of these is NOT written as part of the reactant side of an equation?
2725.explanation: Heat is energy and is normally shown above the arrow or as a separate term, not as a chemical reactant.

options.why: A metal being consumed is a genuine reactant.

options.text: an acid that is used up
options.why: An acid being consumed is a genuine reactant.
Where water actually reacts it is written as a reactant.

2725.stem: In 2H2 + O2 -> 2H2O, the reactants are
2725.explanation: Hydrogen and oxygen are on the left of the arrow, so both are reactants, and water is the only product.

options.why: Water is on the right, so it is the product.
Mixes a reactant with the product.
Mixes a reactant with the product.

2725.stem: The number of reactants in a decomposition reaction is usually
2725.explanation: Decomposition begins with a single compound that breaks down, so there is normally just one reactant.

options.why: Two reactants is the usual pattern for combination or displacement.
Three reactants is uncommon and does not describe decomposition.
Four reactants is very rare and is unrelated to decomposition.

2725.stem: 6 g of carbon reacts completely with 16 g of oxygen. The mass of carbon dioxide formed is
2725.explanation: By conservation of mass the product's mass equals the total mass of the reactants, which is 6 plus 16.

options.why: Uses only the mass of oxygen and ignores the carbon.
Subtracts the masses instead of adding them.
Uses only the mass of carbon and ignores the oxygen.

2725.stem: In the reaction of iron with copper sulphate, which substance is BOTH consumed and part of a product?
2725.explanation: The sulphate group is consumed as copper sulphate but reappears combined with iron in iron sulphate.

options.why: Iron is consumed as a free metal and appears only combined afterwards, not as itself.
Copper begins combined and is set free, which is the opposite pattern.
Water is the solvent and is not consumed in this reaction.

2725.stem: In a sealed flask a reaction produces a gas. The reading on the balance
2725.explanation: Nothing can leave a sealed flask, so the total mass of reactants and products together stays exactly the same.

options.why: The gas is still inside the flask and still on the balance.
Nothing enters the flask, so mass cannot rise.
There is no mechanism for mass to change at all in a sealed vessel.

2725.stem: A student says the reactants in photosynthesis are sunlight and chlorophyll. The correct reactants are
2725.explanation: Carbon dioxide and water are the chemical reactants; sunlight supplies energy and chlorophyll acts as the catalyst.

options.why: These are the products of photosynthesis, not the reactants.
Sunlight is energy and chlorophyll is a catalyst; neither is consumed as a reactant.
Oxygen is produced rather than consumed in photosynthesis.

2725.stem: When lead nitrate is heated, three products form. If one is oxygen and one is nitrogen dioxide, the third must contain
2725.explanation: Lead must appear somewhere among the products, and it does so as lead oxide.

options.why: The nitrogen is already accounted for in the nitrogen dioxide.
No hydrogen is present anywhere in lead nitrate.
No carbon is present anywhere in lead nitrate.

2725.stem: In an open beaker, a reaction that gives off a gas appears to lose mass because
2725.explanation: The gas escapes into the room and is no longer on the balance, though its mass still exists.

options.text: the gas escapes and is no longer weighed
mass is destroyed in the reaction
options.why: Mass is never destroyed in a chemical reaction.
Gases have mass; that is precisely why the reading drops.

options.text: the balance cannot read small masses
options.why: The loss is real and reproducible, not an instrument limitation.

2725.stem: Which change would make a substance stop being described as a reactant?
2725.explanation: If the substance is recovered completely unchanged, it took no chemical part and is at most a catalyst or spectator.

options.text: It is present in a small amount
options.why: Quantity does not decide the role; a limiting reactant is still a reactant.

options.text: It is a liquid rather than a solid
options.why: Physical state is irrelevant to the role a substance plays.

options.text: It is added last to the mixture
options.why: Order of addition does not change what is consumed.

2725.stem: A reaction has two reactants and two products, one of which is water. The reaction is most likely
2725.explanation: Acid and base giving a salt and water is the classic neutralisation, which fits two reactants and two products exactly.

options.why: Decomposition begins with one reactant, not two.
Combination gives a single product, not two.
Photolysis is a decomposition driven by light and starts from one compound.

2725.stem: 10 g of a compound decomposes into 6 g of a solid and some gas. The mass of gas released is
2725.explanation: Conservation of mass requires the gas to make up the difference between 10 g and 6 g.

options.why: Adds the two masses rather than subtracting them.
Repeats the mass of the solid instead of finding the remainder.
Uses the whole starting mass and leaves nothing for the solid.

2725.stem: Which of these best explains why a product cannot also be listed as a reactant in the same simple equation?
2725.explanation: The two sides record the state of the system before and after the change, so the same substance cannot be both unless it is unchanged, which would make it a spectator.

options.text: The sides record before and after the change
It would make the equation too long
options.why: Length is a matter of convenience, not of meaning.
A substance can appear on both sides in some equations, but then it is cancelled as a spectator.
The arrow indicates direction and imposes no rule about repetition.

2725.stem: In the thermite reaction, aluminium and iron oxide give aluminium oxide and iron. The reactant that is reduced is
2725.explanation: Iron oxide loses its oxygen to aluminium, and loss of oxygen is reduction.

options.why: Aluminium gains oxygen, so it is oxidised.
Iron is a product here, not a reactant.
Aluminium oxide is a product here, not a reactant.

2725.stem: A closed system is one in which
2725.explanation: No matter enters or leaves a closed system, which is why conservation of mass can be demonstrated within it.

options.why: That describes an isolated system; a closed system can still exchange energy.
Reversibility concerns the chemistry, not the boundary of the system.
Reactions occur readily in closed systems; only matter is confined.

2725.stem: If a reaction is written A + B -> C and 5 g of A reacts with 7 g of B but only 10 g of C is collected, the most likely explanation is
2725.explanation: Product has been lost during transfer or collection; the chemistry still conserves mass even when the experimenter does not recover it all.

options.text: some product was lost in handling
mass was destroyed in the reaction
options.why: Chemical reactions never destroy mass.

options.text: the law of conservation of mass failed
options.why: The law is not violated by an incomplete recovery.

options.text: A and B were weighed twice
options.why: Double weighing would give a larger figure, not a smaller one.

2725.stem: A student argues that in 'Zn + CuSO4 -> ZnSO4 + Cu' the sulphate should be called a catalyst because it appears on both sides. The most accurate response is
2725.explanation: A species present on both sides unchanged is a spectator ion, not a catalyst, because it does not speed the reaction or take part in the mechanism.

options.text: it is a spectator ion, not a catalyst
the student is right, it is a catalyst
options.why: A catalyst must alter the rate; the sulphate simply remains uninvolved.

options.text: it is a reactant, since it appears on the left
options.why: It is not consumed, so it fails the test for a reactant.

options.text: it is a product, since it appears on the right
options.why: It is not formed by the reaction, so it fails the test for a product.

2725.stem: Two experiments start with the same reactants but give different products. The most likely cause is that
2725.explanation: Conditions such as temperature, concentration or the presence of a catalyst can direct the same reactants down different paths.

options.text: the law of conservation of mass failed
options.why: Conservation of mass holds in both cases regardless of which products form.
The question states both started with the same reactants.
Products are determined by chemistry and conditions, never by chance.

2725.stem: Why does calling a substance 'the limiting reactant' tell you something the equation alone cannot?
2725.explanation: The equation gives fixed ratios, but which reactant runs out first depends on the amounts actually taken, which is experimental information.

options.text: It depends on the amounts actually taken

options.why: The products are the same; only how much forms changes.

options.text: It reverses the direction of reaction
options.why: Running out of a reactant stops the reaction rather than reversing it.

options.text: It shows which reactant is more reactive
options.why: Being limiting is about quantity, not about reactivity.

2725.stem: A reaction is repeated in an open dish and the mass increases. The most reasonable inference is that
2725.explanation: Mass can only rise if something from the surroundings has joined the sample, and oxygen from the air is the usual candidate.

options.text: a gas from the air combined with the sample
mass was created in the reaction
options.why: Mass is never created in a chemical reaction.
Possible in principle, but a real and repeatable gain points to chemistry first.

options.text: a gas escaped from the dish
options.why: Escaping gas would lower the reading, not raise it.

2725.stem: Which statement about reactants and products best explains why burning wood seems to break conservation of mass?
2725.explanation: The gaseous products, mainly carbon dioxide and water vapour, disperse into the air and are never weighed, so only the ash is compared with the wood.

options.text: The gaseous products disperse and are not weighed

options.why: Wood obviously has mass, which is why it can be weighed before burning.

options.text: Ash is heavier than the original wood
options.why: Ash is much lighter, which is the very appearance being explained.
Burning forms new substances and is firmly a chemical change.

2725.stem: In the equation A + 2B -> 3C, doubling the amount of A while keeping B fixed will
2725.explanation: Once B runs out no further product can form, so B becomes limiting and the amount of C does not double.

options.text: not double the amount of C formed
double the amount of C formed
options.why: Ignores that B is now in short supply and will run out first.

options.text: halve the amount of C formed
options.why: Adding more of a reactant cannot reduce the product below its previous level.
The identities of the products are fixed by the chemistry, not by the amounts.

2725.stem: A chemist writes an equation in which an element appears on the left as a free element and on the right inside a compound. This element has
2725.explanation: Going from a free element into a compound means it has combined with something, which is the pattern of oxidation in a displacement or combination reaction.

options.why: Displacement describes the opposite move, from combined to free.
A catalyst ends unchanged, so it cannot end up combined.
A spectator is identical on both sides, which is not the case here.

2725.stem: Which is the strongest reason for writing physical states in an equation alongside reactants and products?
2725.explanation: States show at once which product leaves as a gas or settles as a precipitate, which is the information needed to predict what will actually be observed.

options.text: They predict what will be observed

options.why: Balancing depends on atom counts and is unaffected by state symbols.
The formulae already identify every substance.
Rate is not conveyed by any part of a chemical equation.

2725.stem: In a reaction between a solid and a solution, the solid disappears entirely and no new solid appears. The best conclusion is that
2725.explanation: The solid has been converted into soluble products that remain dissolved in the solution.

options.why: Matter is not destroyed; the atoms are now in the solution.
A solid disappearing into a solution in which it was insoluble indicates a reaction.
Solids in contact with a solution dissolve or react; they do not evaporate.

2725.stem: A student proposes that any substance whose mass falls during a reaction must be a reactant. The flaw in this reasoning is that
2725.explanation: A product can also leave the system, for example as an escaping gas, so a falling mass does not by itself identify a reactant.

options.text: a product can also leave the system

options.why: Reactant masses do fall, which is why the reasoning seems plausible.
Mass is among the most accurately measurable quantities in the laboratory.
Catalysts are precisely the species whose mass does not change.

2725.stem: Why is 'reactant' a better term than 'ingredient' in chemistry?
2725.explanation: An ingredient may simply be mixed in and remain itself, whereas a reactant is chemically consumed and becomes something new.

options.text: An ingredient is only used about food
options.why: The word is used far more widely, so this is not the chemical distinction.

options.text: A reactant must always be perfectly pure
options.why: Purity is a separate matter and reactants are often impure.

options.text: An ingredient can never be weighed out
options.why: Ingredients are weighed routinely, so this is simply untrue.

2725.stem: An equation shows four products where a student expected two. Before concluding the equation is wrong, the best check is
2725.explanation: Counting the atoms of each element on both sides tests whether the equation is consistent, which matters more than how many products were expected.

options.text: count the atoms on each side

options.why: The number of products is not in itself evidence of an error.

options.text: check the order of the products
options.why: Order carries no chemical meaning.

options.text: check whether the arrow is long enough
options.why: The length of the arrow is purely a matter of handwriting.

2725.stem: Two reactions have identical reactants and identical products but different rates. The difference must lie in
2725.explanation: With identity fixed on both sides, only conditions such as temperature, surface area, concentration or a catalyst can account for a different rate.

options.text: the conditions, such as temperature or a catalyst
the law of conservation of mass
options.why: Conservation of mass holds identically in both and says nothing about rate.
The products are stated to be identical.
Both proceed in the same direction, since both have the same products.

2726.stem: A chemical equation written with formulae instead of names is called
2726.explanation: Replacing the names in a word equation with the corresponding chemical formulae gives a chemical or symbol equation.

options.why: A word equation uses names, which is exactly what has been replaced.
A formula unit is a single substance's formula, not a whole equation.
A structural diagram shows how atoms are bonded within one molecule.

2726.stem: The formula of water is
2726.explanation: Each water molecule contains two hydrogen atoms bonded to one oxygen atom, giving H2O.

options.why: Reverses the subscripts and describes a different species altogether.
This is hydrogen peroxide, a different compound.
This is the hydroxide group, not a complete water molecule.

2726.stem: In the formula CaCO3, the number of oxygen atoms is
2726.explanation: The subscript 3 after O shows three oxygen atoms in each formula unit of calcium carbonate.

options.why: Ignores the subscript that follows the oxygen symbol.
Misreads the subscript attached to the oxygen.
Doubles the subscript without any reason to do so.

2726.stem: The formula for carbon dioxide is
2726.explanation: Carbon dioxide contains one carbon atom joined to two oxygen atoms, written CO2.

options.why: This is carbon monoxide, a different and poisonous gas.
Places the subscript on the wrong element.
This is calcium oxide, an entirely different compound.

2726.stem: Writing an equation in formulae rather than words allows chemists to
2726.explanation: Formulae carry the number of atoms of each element, so amounts can be counted and calculated.

options.why: Names are clearer in a word equation; formulae add quantity, not clarity of naming.

options.text: show the colour of each substance
options.why: Colour is never shown by a chemical formula.

options.text: show how fast the reaction goes
options.why: Rate is not conveyed by any chemical equation.

2726.stem: In 2H2O, the large number 2 in front is called
2726.explanation: A number written before a formula is the coefficient, and it multiplies every atom in that formula.

options.why: A subscript is the small number written below and after a symbol.
Index is a mathematical term for a power, not for a chemical coefficient.
Valency is the combining capacity of an element, a different idea.

2726.stem: The formula of sodium chloride is
2726.explanation: Sodium and chlorine combine in a one-to-one ratio, giving the formula NaCl.

options.why: Sodium has a valency of one, so it combines with only one chlorine.
Chlorine has a valency of one, so only one sodium is needed.
This is sodium hypochlorite, which contains oxygen as well.

2726.stem: 2Na means
2726.explanation: The coefficient 2 placed before the symbol means two separate atoms of sodium.

options.text: one molecule with two sodiums bonded
options.why: Bonded atoms would be written Na2, with the number as a subscript.

options.text: sodium with a valency of two
options.why: Valency is not shown by a number written in front of a symbol.
Position in the periodic table is not written this way.

2726.stem: In H2SO4, the total number of atoms in one formula unit is
2726.explanation: Two hydrogen plus one sulphur plus four oxygen gives seven atoms in total.

options.why: Counts only the oxygen atoms.
Counts the three different elements rather than the atoms.
Misses one of the atoms in the count.

2726.stem: Which formula represents an element rather than a compound?
2726.explanation: O2 contains only one kind of atom, so it is an element, even though it is a molecule.

options.why: Contains two different elements, so it is a compound.
Contains two different elements, so it is a compound.
Contains two different elements, so it is a compound.

2726.stem: The formula of calcium oxide, or quick lime, is
2726.explanation: Calcium and oxygen both have a valency of two, so they combine one to one to give CaO.

options.why: Oxygen's valency of two is satisfied by a single calcium atom.
Calcium's valency of two is satisfied by a single oxygen atom.
This is calcium carbonate, which is limestone rather than quick lime.

2726.stem: Changing a subscript in a formula while balancing an equation is not allowed because it
2726.explanation: Subscripts define the identity of the substance, so altering one turns it into a different compound.

options.why: Length is irrelevant; the objection is that the chemistry changes.
Conditions are written above the arrow and are unaffected by subscripts.
Readability is not the reason for the rule.

2726.stem: In 3CaCO3, the total number of calcium atoms is
2726.explanation: The coefficient 3 multiplies everything in the formula, and each formula unit has one calcium atom.

options.why: Ignores the coefficient written in front.
Multiplies the coefficient by the oxygen subscript instead.
Uses a subscript that does not apply to calcium.

2726.stem: The formula for hydrogen gas as it exists in nature is
2726.explanation: Hydrogen is diatomic, so free hydrogen gas is written H2.

options.why: A single hydrogen atom does not exist freely under ordinary conditions.
Hydrogen molecules contain two atoms, not three.
This means two separate atoms, not one molecule of the gas.

2726.stem: The word equation 'zinc + hydrochloric acid -> zinc chloride + hydrogen' written in formulae is
2726.explanation: Zinc chloride is ZnCl2 and hydrogen is diatomic, so two molecules of acid are needed to supply both chlorine atoms and the hydrogen molecule.

options.why: One HCl cannot supply the two chlorine atoms in ZnCl2.
Zinc has a valency of two, so the chloride must be ZnCl2.
Hydrogen gas is diatomic and is written H2, not as free atoms.

2726.stem: Which is the correct formula equation for the burning of magnesium?
2726.explanation: Oxygen is diatomic, so two magnesium atoms are needed to use both oxygen atoms, giving two units of magnesium oxide.

options.why: Free oxygen exists as O2, not as single atoms.
Magnesium and oxygen both have a valency of two, so the formula is MgO.
Leaves two oxygen atoms unaccounted for on the product side.

2726.stem: Converting 'calcium hydroxide + carbon dioxide -> calcium carbonate + water' into formulae gives calcium hydroxide as
2726.explanation: Calcium has a valency of two and hydroxide has a valency of one, so two hydroxide groups are needed and are enclosed in brackets.

options.why: Leaves calcium's second valency unsatisfied.
Without brackets the 2 applies only to hydrogen, which is a different species.
Reverses which part needs to be doubled.

2726.stem: In the equation Fe2O3 + 2Al -> Al2O3 + 2Fe, the number of iron atoms on the left is
2726.explanation: The subscript 2 in Fe2O3 shows two iron atoms, and there is no coefficient to multiply it.

options.why: Ignores the subscript attached to the iron.
Reads the oxygen subscript instead of the iron subscript.
Applies the coefficient of aluminium to the iron.

2726.stem: The formula equation for the decomposition of water by electricity is
2726.explanation: Two water molecules give two hydrogen molecules and one oxygen molecule, which is the two-to-one volume ratio observed in electrolysis.

options.why: Oxygen is released as O2, not as single atoms.
Both gases are diatomic and should be written as molecules.
Not balanced: there are far more atoms on the right than on the left.

2726.stem: Why is Na2SO4 written with the 2 as a subscript after Na rather than as a coefficient in front?
2726.explanation: The two sodium atoms are part of one formula unit, so the number belongs as a subscript; a coefficient would mean two separate units.

options.text: The two sodiums belong to one formula unit
Coefficients are only used for elements
options.why: Coefficients are used with compounds all the time.
Typography has nothing to do with chemical meaning.
Balancing is done with coefficients, never by adjusting subscripts.

2726.stem: Which formula equation correctly represents 'barium chloride + sodium sulphate -> barium sulphate + sodium chloride'?
2726.explanation: Barium and sulphate both have a valency of two, so barium sulphate is BaSO4, and two sodium chlorides balance the two chlorines.

options.why: Both barium chloride and sodium sulphate have wrong formulae here.
Invents formulae that do not match the valencies of the ions.
Sodium sulphate needs two sodium atoms to balance the sulphate.

2726.stem: A student writes 'H2 + O2 -> H2O2' for the formation of water. The error is that
2726.explanation: H2O2 is hydrogen peroxide; water is H2O, so the student has written a different compound entirely.

options.text: H2O2 is a different compound from water
hydrogen should be written as H
options.why: Hydrogen gas is correctly written as the diatomic H2.

options.text: oxygen should be written as O
options.why: Oxygen gas is correctly written as the diatomic O2.

options.text: the arrow should point the other way
options.why: Hydrogen and oxygen are the reactants, so the arrow direction is correct.

2726.stem: In 2Ca(OH)2, the total number of hydrogen atoms is
2726.explanation: Each formula unit has two hydroxide groups with one hydrogen each, and the coefficient 2 doubles that to four.

options.why: Applies either the coefficient or the bracket subscript, but not both.
Counts only the hydrogen written inside the bracket once.
Multiplies by an extra factor that is not present.

2726.stem: Writing 'sodium carbonate' in formulae requires knowing that the carbonate group is
2726.explanation: Carbonate is CO3 with a valency of two, so two sodium atoms are needed, giving Na2CO3.

options.text: CO3 with a valency of two
CO2 with a valency of one
options.why: CO2 is carbon dioxide, a molecule, not the carbonate group.

options.text: CO with a valency of two
options.why: CO is carbon monoxide, not the carbonate group.

options.text: C with a valency of four
options.why: That is carbon's own valency, not the charge of the carbonate group.

2726.stem: Which of the following is written correctly with brackets?
2726.explanation: Brackets are needed whenever a group of more than one atom must be multiplied, so aluminium sulphate is Al2(SO4)3.

options.why: Without brackets the 3 applies only to the oxygen count, changing the group.
Brackets around a single element serve no purpose.
Places a coefficient inside the bracket, which is not how formulae are written.

2726.stem: The main risk in converting a word equation to formulae is
2726.explanation: A formula written with the wrong valency produces a substance that does not exist, and the equation then describes chemistry that never happens.

options.text: getting a valency wrong and inventing a substance

options.why: The number of plus signs follows directly from the number of substances.

options.text: putting the arrow in the middle
options.why: The middle is exactly where the arrow belongs.
Names are replaced by formulae, so brevity of names is irrelevant.

2726.stem: CuSO4 + Zn -> ZnSO4 + Cu. The sulphate group here behaves as
2726.explanation: The SO4 group passes from copper to zinc unchanged, acting as a single unit throughout.

options.why: The group stays bonded together and is not broken apart.
It changes partner rather than remaining entirely uninvolved.
Sulphate is a group of bonded atoms, not an element.

2726.stem: A student balances an equation by changing H2O to H2O2 and declares it balanced. The most serious objection is that
2726.explanation: Changing a subscript changes the substance, so the equation now describes a different reaction, no matter how well the atoms count up.

options.text: the equation now describes a different reaction
the equation is still not balanced
options.why: The objection stands even if the atom counts happen to work out.

options.text: coefficients should be written as fractions
options.why: Fractions are sometimes used but are not the issue here.
Stability is a property of the compound, not the reason the method is wrong.

2726.stem: Why does writing formulae make the law of conservation of mass checkable in a way word equations never are?
2726.explanation: Formulae give the number of atoms of each element, so both sides can be counted and compared; names carry no counts to compare.

options.text: Formulae give countable atoms on both sides

options.why: Brevity has no bearing on whether mass can be checked.
States are shown by separate symbols and do not help count atoms.
Catalysts are written above the arrow and do not enter the atom count.

2726.stem: Two students write the same reaction as Ca + O2 -> CaO and 2Ca + O2 -> 2CaO. The correct assessment is
2726.explanation: Both use correct formulae, but only the second conserves atoms; the first leaves one oxygen atom unaccounted for.

options.text: both of them are equally acceptable
options.why: An unbalanced equation implies atoms disappear, which cannot happen.

options.text: only the first one is acceptable
options.why: The first has one oxygen atom left over on the reactant side.
Ca, O2 and CaO are all written correctly.

2726.stem: Which explains why Fe2O3 cannot be written FeO3 even though both contain oxygen?
2726.explanation: The subscripts follow from the valencies of iron and oxygen, and FeO3 would require iron to have a valency of six, which it does not show here.

options.text: The subscripts are fixed by the valencies involved
Iron oxide must always have two metal atoms
options.why: FeO exists with one iron atom, so this is not a general rule.

options.text: Oxygen cannot have a subscript of three
options.why: Oxygen carries a subscript of three in several correct formulae.

options.text: Formulae are chosen by convention alone
options.why: Formulae reflect actual combining ratios, not arbitrary choice.

2726.stem: An equation is written entirely in correct formulae but describes a reaction that does not occur. This shows that
2726.explanation: Correct formulae and correct balancing guarantee internal consistency only; whether a reaction happens is decided by experiment and by chemical principles such as reactivity.

options.text: correct notation does not guarantee the reaction happens
the formulae must be wrong after all
options.why: The question stipulates the formulae are correct.

options.text: every balanced equation describes a real reaction
options.why: This is exactly the belief the example refutes.
Equations describe real reactions routinely; the point is that not every one written is real.

2726.stem: Converting a complex word equation to formulae, the step most likely to introduce an error that balancing will NOT reveal is
2726.explanation: A wrong formula can still be balanced successfully, so the mistake survives the check; balancing tests atom counts, not identity.

options.text: assigning a wrong formula to a substance
writing the arrow the wrong way
options.why: A reversed arrow is usually obvious from the description given.
A missing plus sign is visible immediately in the written equation.

options.text: using a coefficient that is too large
options.why: Balancing checks precisely this and will show the discrepancy.

2726.stem: Why can the same element appear with different subscripts in different compounds?
2726.explanation: The ratio depends on the valencies of both elements in that particular compound, and many elements show more than one valency.

options.text: Combining ratios depend on the valencies in that compound
Subscripts are chosen to make equations balance
options.why: Subscripts are fixed by the compound; only coefficients may be adjusted.

options.text: Elements change their identity between compounds
options.why: An element's identity is fixed by its atomic number.
Chemical formulae are internationally standardised.

2726.stem: In Al2(SO4)3 the total number of oxygen atoms is
2726.explanation: Each sulphate group contains four oxygen atoms and there are three such groups, giving twelve oxygen atoms.

options.why: Counts one sulphate group and ignores the bracket subscript.
Adds the two subscripts instead of multiplying them.
Reads only the number outside the bracket.

2726.stem: A chemist replaces every name in a word equation with a formula and finds the equation balances first time with no coefficients. The most reasonable conclusion is
2726.explanation: Some reactions genuinely balance with all coefficients equal to one, so this is possible and is not by itself evidence of an error.

options.text: some reactions do balance with unit coefficients
the formulae must contain a mistake
options.why: Balancing at once is common and is not suspicious in itself.
Most equations require coefficients greater than one somewhere.
Coefficients are essential in the great majority of equations.

2726.stem: Which statement best captures the relationship between a word equation and its formula equation?
2726.explanation: The formula equation carries everything the word equation says and adds quantitative information about the atoms involved.

options.text: The formula equation says the same and more
They carry exactly the same information
options.why: Formulae add atom counts that names cannot express.
The word equation is strictly the less informative of the two.
Both describe the same reaction, in different notation.

2726.stem: A formula equation contains a substance written as NaCl2. Before balancing, the correct action is
2726.explanation: Sodium has a valency of one, so NaCl2 does not exist; the formula must be corrected to NaCl before any balancing is attempted.

options.text: leave the equation exactly as it stands
options.why: Balancing a wrong formula produces a correct-looking but meaningless equation.

options.text: add a coefficient in front of NaCl2
options.why: A coefficient cannot repair a formula that describes no real substance.
Sodium genuinely takes part and cannot simply be dropped.

2726.stem: Why is knowing the diatomic elements essential when writing formula equations?
2726.explanation: Elements such as hydrogen, oxygen, nitrogen and the halogens exist as two-atom molecules, and writing them as single atoms gives the wrong atom count on that side.

options.text: Writing them as single atoms gives a wrong atom count
They cannot appear in equations at all
options.why: They appear in equations constantly, written as molecules.
Brackets are for groups of different atoms, not for diatomic elements.
They frequently carry coefficients, as in 2H2 or 3O2.

2726.stem: Two formula equations for the same reaction differ only in that one has every coefficient doubled. The correct assessment is
2726.explanation: Both are balanced and describe the same chemistry, but convention prefers the smallest whole-number set of coefficients.

options.text: both are balanced, but the smaller set is preferred

options.why: It conserves atoms perfectly well, so it is not wrong, only unconventional.
Doubling every coefficient changes scale, not chemistry.

options.text: only the doubled one is balanced
options.why: If one is balanced, so is the other.
